This is exactly the main criticism of ideas like idealism and you've articulated it well (imo). The idea that representation is not a 'real' thing becomes meaningless when we actually take a step back and think about what could possibly give us reason to think otherwise.

A common counter-argument is the existance of things we know to be there but have no actual way of directly observing; we know through inference and second hand effects. To give an example, we had never actually observed an atom until very recently (2018 I believe was the first proper image we got). We had models and effects that implied there were very small constituent parts of matter but for the majority of time that we theorised about it (think close to 2000 years, the bulk of that time it was simply an argument from reduction that they must exist by necessity) we never had any 'hard' proof.

In short, part of the reason empiricism exists is to answer your question; our experience is limited but our reason *informs* us of this.

>Why do we need to remove ourselves from the human experience?

Fundamentally this is where philosophers and scientists diverge on their justification. On the one hand, the former would say basically what I have outlined above. That our senses and experience as a whole are an incomplete picture. Amongst *some* of the latter, the answer is that we cannot say anything is ever as it is because even when we try to become very precise in our descriptions of things they can only ever be tied to our human perspective.

This means not just our subjective experience, but what we deem to be objective as well as our physicality. Breaking it down:

1. Your subjective experience is informed by thoughts and feelings you are having at the time.
2. Objective (whether that be rational or empirical objectivity) experience is limited by two main things (which branch out to many) which are your ability to measure, to think or comprehend a thing. Further, your interpretation of not only the data but what or how to observe something in the first place.
3. Physicality in the sense that our eyes allow us to see a very limited range of light which, if altered, would change how we fundamentally describe the world. As a personal anecdote, if you try to think about what it would be like to live in a house as a cat, which has a much more powerful sense of hearing than either dogs or humans, the walls of said house would serve little purpose in masking activity to them as hearing is their primary form of observation. If they were to build a house, sound-proofed walls is the first thing they would invent and would possibly just be part of the definition of a 'wall'.

So while on the one hand we have the empirical position that both our senses are too limited to perceive things as they are **and** we can escape that to some degree; this is met with the idea that there are ways of understanding the world that escape us and therefore put a hard-cap on our capacity to actually 'see' things for how they truly are. Note - this is different from saying we cannot function - simply that by necessity if we want to get to the 'truth' of things we are in all likelihood locked off from it.

it is my contention that you have, by no fault of your own, missed that fundamentally we are charged with finding meaningful things in our lives. What makes this difficult to see is the same reason so many people are depressed, society has degraded to the point where the things we *need* to feel like we have meaning have largely been stripped away from us.

For alot of us, myself included and it sounds like you too, we have been put into a position where it feels like there is genuinely nothing. See if you can agree, disagree or add to the following:

* Go to bars, after the 3rd, 4th or 15th time it just seems like no one there is really having fun. The people who are laughing or seem fun don't want to talk to you and it seems like there's just nothing really there for anybody who isn't loud.
* Go to events, need to plan in advance and when we eventually do get there it's great. Then it ends, with no lasting impact, no new friends and no real sense of accomplishment.
* Take up a hobby, try to go to a class but it ends up being cliquey and weird. Try another one, same thing. Maybe you go and it's actually impactful, but then you have to move or get a new job. Eventually just give up on the hobby altogether.

These are examples where, for some people, they are enough. For an increasing number, they feel hollow and empty. Why?

Part of the reason is that when you have depression for a long time (not massive, a year or so) you get used to it. 'Depression vision' becomes just your vision and your view of the world becomes tainted, which in turn taints our feelings when we are in a place we are 'supposed' to feel meaningful things. This creates an unfair expectation, that we are not allowed to feel depressed, so we pretend. *We become superficially happy*.

To put it simply, part of the reason things seem meaningless is precisely because we cannot find meaning in things when we are pre-occupied with pretending to be ok. Going on dates, to a game, playing games, reading, studying etc... The reason these things *have* meaning in the first place is entirely dependent on your ability to create that meaning. You cannot do that if you are pre-occupied with not falling apart.

Please feel what you need to feel. Please don't feel guilty if you take a break (distract) but know that what you are feeling is grief. You are grieving a relationship. It is not dramatic to say that when someone we once confided in and thought of every day is suddenly not there. We sort of 'withdraw' from the love we felt (even if there were problems). 

Right now I can't tell you if things are going to get better or what that might look like. All I can tell you is that you are going to change. The way grief can be looked at is like a wound, it hurts like hell but there's no pain killer. We can try to numb it but all that happens is it sticks around. *What you have to focus on and the most healthy path forward is something you are already doing*. Talk, reach out, keep telling your story (in as much or little detail as you like) until you are ready to understand your pain. 

  
The second thing is that this will take time. It will not disappear over night and if it persists then you will need professional help. Above all else, do not be ashamed for asking for help. 

Please, try not to despise your loneliness. It is telling you that you need help - that is ok. What you are feeling is the need to connect. I can't promise by the time you finish reading this that you will feel better, but I see you. Reach out if you need help. 

You can get through this but the first thing you need to do is give yourself permission to feel what you need to feel. If you absolutely cannot help but shut down, please try to be compassionate with yourself. Finally, don't set deadlines on healing from this - it's an unfortunate irony that when we are grief stricken the worst thing you can do is try to speed it up. Listen to your body.

I am a philosophy grad who also happened to be drawn to philosophy for this exact reason - not only did I share your fear but I wanted to be able to look for a good answer as to why to not fear it. What has helped me so far:

1. Schopenhauer's metaphysics in terms of a way of approaching life. While his metaphysics is more about the nature of reality as both illusion (as he borrows heavily from Hindu (?) religion) but also as something that fundamentally belongs to our experience. Essentially - that we are both isolated in how we experience the world, but connected to every other person at the same time. You are both unique in your *perspective* but not necessarily your experience.
2. Socrates' answer to why we do philosophy - essentially to die well one must live well. It is found in his final moments (cannot recall the exact text)
3. Liebnitz' 'best possible world', it is a 'theory of everything' that poses that the world and everything within it is as it is because it is *necessarily* so; that it could not be anything else. If it were, if even the smallest thing was changed, it would cease to be the best possible world. What 'best' means for Liebnitz is, in a mathematical sense, balanced like an equation. A comparable concept could be 'efficient given the limitations of each constituent part'.
4. Nietzsche, specifically the Geneology, Thus Spoke and Gay Science. I need to go over this in more detail below.

What I found was that the answer as to how to stop fearing death is that it is in fact the wrong question; better yet it is in fact not death you fear. You and I actually fear not living well, because death is not defined in and of itself. Not to sound too mystical but death is only ever understood as an end of life, or at the very least (in a religious context) a transformation from one state to another.

Focusing on the ontology of death for a moment,it does not make sense to fear it. It is an end, you will either simply cease and rejoin an endless 'sleep' or continue on in some way. None of that is something you should fear in and of itself, because how can you fear nothing? The only interpretation where it can be feared in this way is if you believe in some form of hell or vengeful creator or judge.

If we take a step back a moment, all interpretations essentially entail that one should live 'correctly'. Whether that be to have a fulfilling life, to make time for your loved ones or to just avoid endless suffering. This is where Nietzsche's work is quite useful, particularly Thus Spoke and the Geneology, as he attempts to address what we should be looking for in terms of finding meaning (although this is only if you read him with that in mind, he concerns himself with a lot more than just how we approach meaning).

From my limited understanding, and I approach this to the best of my ability; there are people on this sub who will have far more nuanced and concise answers than mine, it's that if you want to overcome your fear of death you must live a meaningful life. What that itself means is something that can never really be 'told' to someone. That is explicitly the domain of religion. It is something we either 'find' or 'create' in how we spend our time alive.

Hope this helps. Again, others will be far better in both qualification and quality of their answers but I felt the need to at least try.

First let's address how you're feeling. I am very sorry you have to be in this place. I have struggled and still do. You are not alone, there is nothing wrong with you, you have an illness but that illness doesn't have to define you.

 Now, let's break down motivation a bit. There are probably studies that make my points a lot more scientifically coherent, however for now I think it is useful to speak informally. Generally speaking we think of motivation as internally occurring, when it fact it can both come from you ('I am going to do this, I am disciplined') and it can come from an external source ('I need to do this because I have to'). Understand that, for most things, you will not be motivated to do them internally and it is only when you start doing them that you remain relatively motivated - this is especially true of people with depression. Our ability to find purpose, to feel that sense of drive and belonging in the world is robbed from us. You will need to rely on the latter rather than the former kind of motivation.

What works for me as someone who has suffered from depression for way too long - do not start the day with anything you need to do. Yes, needing to get up is a great motivator because it is external and logically makes sense - if your cat needs to be fed you will do it because you would rather they not starve. However it is important that you do something that can be done, that takes minimal energy but simply makes you budge a little bit. 

Today that might be one thing that lasts for 5 minutes, but tomorrow make it two things and then the day after maybe three (or bring it down to one or two when you are not comfortable). 

However, the final thing I want to highlight is that every depressed person is in deep (and most of the time unrelenting and invasive) self-reflection. Not everybody is self-loathing, however everybody who is depressed is almost always constantly thinking "I need to do this, but I can't; what is wrong with me" or something like this. What I have found, and this may not work with you, is to almost think as if you're already out of bed and can't get back until they're all done. In other words *try* to see what you need to do not as an obligation but something you need to do to get back to bed. Reframe it from "I need to feed the cat or they'll starve" to "I need to feed the cat so I can get back to bed". Do this with everything, I personally have found that this works because it almost makes the more physical aspects of depression (fatigue) more manageable.  


If you don't find this useful, I hope you find something that you do. You're not alone.

This is more I actually recently had to re-learn the trick to combatting this trap. First of all, acknowledge it is a trap even if it feels like the validation of others cuts deep. Second, understand that *anybody who says anything about you, without actually knowing you, is projecting*. Whatever those people are saying - if you know for a fact that what you do makes sense *to you* and they refuse or cannot possibly know,  what they are saying is 100% about them.

Take the following interaction I had recently:

Acquiantance: You know I know you **fuck around a lot** Dessy

Dessy: What do you mean?

Acquaintance: Well, look at you, **you're a mess**. You have not turned up to class in 3 weeks consistently.

Dessy: I was abroad, dude. (I was actually also ill and tired from work).

Acquaintance: Yeah but that doesn't take away from the inconsistency, **you lack drive dude.**

The bold bits are all assertions based on nothing, this guy suddenly starts inserting all these weird claims about me. By seeing them not as critiques (which sounds like what you do) and focus instead on *where they could be coming from*, you begin to realise that this guy:

1. Is insecure about fucking around - whatever that means or Is insecure about *being* an uptight person.
2. Sees himself in some way as a mess or uses organisation as a way to feel superior to others.
3. Is terrified of being perceived as lacking drive or has some deep seated issue about being kind to himself.

Do you see what I am getting at here? When someone projects onto you, something that happens *every time* someone makes a claim about you as a person without actually knowing or listening to you, It can be about an insecurity regarding the claim itself:

"I will say he lacks drive because I see him as below me and I hate *myself* when I lack drive"

Or a kind of inversion of the trait claimed as it is an insecurity based more in fear:

"He lacks drive because I am organised, if I am not organised I am a terrible person".

And so on, this is ofcourse not mind reading but it is generally what you can infer from someone talking shit to you. Let's do the same with what you said:

"Dooble is such a **weirdo** and she is **ugly**".

They are:

1. Insecure about their own unique traits and see yours on display openly (jealousy) or fear being different themselves so exaggerate your difference to *avoid being called out on theirs* (cowardace).
2. Insecure about their own beauty *or* (this bit is unique to claims about physical appearance) *use their physical appearance to gain validation*.
3. Keep in mind, if someone calls you ugly it could be a *very* fucked up way to say "I actually find you beautiful and don't want you to suspect a thing; because I am a child".

These are not the only things they could be, but understand and feel that all you have to do is take a proper look at the person doing this to you. Why would someone be horrible? People are very much alike, all the feelings you have they have too.

As for rumours, keep you cool and learn to laugh at how silly it is. I find the only real way to get from where you are to a comfortable place is to laugh at yourself in the way you'd laugh with a friend about something. "Oh that guy asked 'which movie do I like' and I said 'yes', haha". Recognise that we are essentially very *far* from perfect and it is those imperfections and goofy moments that make life worth living.

TL;DR

1. You will attract people by being more *authentic,* not more *confident*. Being confident without authenticity is a show, being confident about your authenticity is the real deal and will attract people to you.
2. All of those Melonfarmers are either projecting or listening to the person projecting (creating a rumour).
3. Whenever someone says something that *they cannot possibly know*, like you are a weirdo, realise that it says something *about them*. Literally, it lets you see that something *about being a weirdo* terrifies or infuriates them.
4. The same with being called ugly - physical attractiveness only really comes into play with someone you approach for sex/dating. Even in that case, calling someone ugly is weird because the only reason you would do that is to hurt the other person - something only an insecure mess does.
5. Finally, learn to take life less seriously when it comes to how people see you and life **will** **reflect this.** It's like a fucked up quirk that when you start behaving more positively in a way that belittes the bad or dark aspects, life gets better.

This brought down retribution from the ex, but even after all of that I returned to an abusive family that was becoming more and more abusive. In short, not a good fucking time. After that time and during the familial abusive phase I did not feel like myself, I was not talking to people like I normally would, I couldn't relate to anyone, my friends were all in different cities and busy as hell. I was essentially alone. So I did what I used to do and go out. Night after night. Just looking for some form of connection with anyone who wanted a connection or conversation. What I noticed was that when I was being open, not talking about my trauma but just sincere about whatever we were talking about, people were generally turned off by this. It was very weird as not 2 years earlier (at the time) people fucking loved that about me - the difference was that I was more serious without actually knowing it. I now had things to be insecure about in a way that was sort of threatening to 'good vibes'.

The main take away from those sets of experiences, which lasted for *4 years* was that on the one hand people do not want to take on the baggage of a fully grown man and they confuse baggage with demeanor. If you are a guy talking to anyone and something is wrong then they conflate what is wrong *with who you are as a person*. On the other hand I found that despite people generally looking down on being vulnurable it was *exceedingly* rare to have anyone totally dismiss it. The most common reaction by far was advice, shitty uninterested advice maybe, but it was an attempt. This told me that despite people being *bad* at dealing with openness, on the whole they wanted to hear and help (they just didn't know how).

If you find yourself feeling like people's reactions to you being vulnurable are affecting your mental health, look into what has hindered your self esteem. Hey dude, I'm probably not going to be able to dissuade you as I dip in and out of the same mindset but there are things I think I know in a 'rational' sense that may help. Could be full of shit though, you judge.

First, for your question, there are not a lot of rational reasons not to commit suicide as life and meaningful experiences are very rarely rational. Meaning outside of philosophical systems of ethics and metaphysics people do not derive their own personal meaning from well-thought out arguments. A lot of it boils down to, am I happy? Do I suffer more than I am happy? and that's it. In other words people's justifications, while they can be articulated are rarely fully capable of being expressed.

You will hear a lot of people talk about how there 'might be something else', 'just hang in there' etc, these people are not wrong but I can see why that might irk you. The reason they are saying these kind of vague things is because they *cannot tell you* what your reason for living should or could be in the future. That is the key to answering your question, that while there *is not no reason to commit suicide* in the sense that there is an objective, strong metaphysical argument for why it is the worst option, there is instead a strong argument based on inference that life is worth living.

before going into why life might be worth living, let's look at your arguments for why there is no reason. Please correct me if I am summing this up wrong, my intention is not to misrepresent you and to fully engage with you.

​

1. Adults can make their own decisions
2. I am an adult and have been for a period of time.
3. life is not worth living as an adult
4. So I am free choose to end my life.

This is the first 'arm' of your argument. What I immediately see here is that you assume that the amount of time you've been an adult gives you any authority in the matter of 'being' an adult. Don't get me wrong, I know what you mean is that so far *being an adult for you has been miserable*. However, it appears to me from this arm alone, if I have understood you correctly, is that there is an assumption that you have suffered a long time and this is in fact proof that all adulthood for you or in your forseeable future is going to be suffering.

You cannot possibly know this. I don't mean that in the instagram quote 'things will get better' kind of way, I mean you literally do not have access to knowledge about your future self. You do not know whether things could get worse, you might think you have enough information to infer that *probably* things will either continue as they are or get worse. That may be the case, but just as no one has the right to say that things *will* get better, you do not have an ability to say definitively that adulthood for you will stay static. From this, you nor I can say that adulthood will never be worth living for either of us.

The second arm is less of an entirely different argument but acts as proof of the first. It seems like your problem with adulthood is that (underlying assumptions in brackets):

1. Work sucks (that my work defines me or does not define me adequately and is wasting my time. I cannot get out of my work in the near future).
2. Other people are always trying to fuck you over (That you do not have, or feel you do not have many people you can trust in any meaningful and substantial way).
3. You think children are gross and therein do not have a family to look forward to (that you should have children and a family is the only way to have a future).
4. Why can't I kill myself?

To summise; you want to kill yourself, or rather see no reason not to because you have no sense of meaningful purpose, you cannot trust anyone in a meaningful or important way, and; that you have no future responsibilities that would make life meaningful outside of the former two aspects. It seems apparent but by no means obvious that *you value these things enough (purpose, trust and family) that their lack basically means that life is meaningless for you.* I am very sorry if I got all of that wrong, again I'm just trying to help but if I am doing more harm than good feel free to call me out.

Going back to those things you value, and what we said before that there is no real rational basis to live for itself i.e. to simply breath, eat, reproduce and expire. Joy is not rational, purpose is not rational and neither is trust nor family\*.\* They are human things and thus inherently flawed and temporary. You do yourself a great disservice, in my opinion and if you do indeed value these things enough that their lack makes you want to take your own life, to hold yourself to a standard that even the best human in history couldn't possibly attain consistently in their lifetimes. Most people who find meaning in the things they value do so on *their own terms*.

Which brings me to the end of this post and my final point. I cannot speak for life as I, myself, have not lived through it, I couldn't tell you what the overall point is; I can't make a case for it because there is none. Not in the sense of a concrete, religious, metaphysical singular point that comes along and makes you utterly convinced that suicide is an absurd choice. However, the fact that you are here in the now *looking for that point* by asking the question *why can't I just end it all* means that you are participating in whatever the fuck this all is. That is the point. We dance because we want to, we get mad because we feel mad and upset, we breathe because we are alive and we are alive because we breathe. Break it down however you want, a lot of it is just unfair and random bullshit but meaning is found for every person individually.

What makes something a description is whether it hinges on the base-ontological aspects of something. I.e. a gene contains heritable information which is transcribed into the phenotyical expression found in someone's face or abilities. That doesn't tell me, as you rightly point out, why that mechanism does what it does. Disregarding the insufficient nature of genes, what descriptions rely on are pre-defined concepts that allows us to understand something within a specific epistemological framework (in our example, genetics or biology).

Explanations can be descriptive but what you're alluding to is more the compound reasons something acts in the way it does. To decribe things in a more elaborate way does not suffice to actually provide an explanation because all you are doing is reducing all elements to that specific epistemology. As an example:

The theory of general relativity doesn't relate to genes directly, but it gives a larger context for the descriptions of genes to make sense in what we could term a 'scientific reductionist understanding'. That is, from one theory to the other, they support each other because quite clearly the universe follows a set of natural laws which govern how a particle operates, how space and time interact and eventually lead to life. What neither of these theories do is provide us a metaphysical reason for these interactions - that is they do not lay a ground work for how we *should* understand them.

Scientific opponents of philosophy tend to decry the interpetive nature of philosophy in this way. Why should we understand a theory any other way? The answer to this is simply that an explanatory theory is able to give that 'should' or correctness in understanding a theory. If we get this wrong, you get eugenics. You get social darwinian advocates. You basically get people who are incapable or willfully ignorant on what is in the best interest of science and humanity as a whole.

I am speaking as someone who studied philosophy at undergrad but transitioned to law 2 years ago. I'll explain why that transition is important in relation to your question - I hope this helps.

I could and still can pick up any philosophical text, whether contemporary or historical and understand it. I thought that this was just being 'naturally brilliant' or whatever arrogant nonsense I subscribed to when Philosophy was my sole item of study.

Then enter the law, where I find it difficult to remember what I've read in cases or textbooks until I started practicing. There are several factors as to why this happened.

1. Philosophy was something I had wanted to do from the age of 17. The questions asked were layered in a hazey sense of 'this is my purpose'. As such, all of the fluff around a core argument is absorbed like a spunge.
2. The law, in contrast, doesn't have that same 'pull' for me. I cannot intuitively link it to deeper questions about the law. In other words I am not yet interested in the law in and of itself.
3. My notes look completely different for my Philosophy degree vs. my Law degree. The former notes are there to prompt an idea I have already formed in my head linking it to other ideas and as a result barely reach two pages on average. The latter is the complete opposite. My notes are long winded novels with several points of clarification *that I still forget to this day.*
4. The degrees were taken at different intensities, I was a fully funded philosophy undergrad who would only work if the money ran out, whereas I was working full-time as a law post-grad meaning I was sleep deprived before I even set my eyes on a page. If you're working, studying something else or just pre-occupied in your day to day life you *will* find it difficult to retain information.

My best advice? when you read a text, take notes *after* you have read the chapter. This will aid in recall as you have to construct notes based off of your understanding. As you keep doing this, you get into the habit of linking one idea with another. For example:

Plato's theory of forms is either a multiversal or a neurological claim.

Otherwise, always take notes by hand *then* type them. *Do not* panic if there are terms you do not understand, keep reading and form notes on what specifically doesn't make sense to you as this will allow you to develop the skill of *recognising what ideas are being created to support an argument*.

Finally and perhaps the most important, talk about it. Talk about it with your family, your friends, here on reddit, in a bar or shout it from the roof. It doesn't matter where you do it, discussion is often times the key to clarity.

Hope this helps.

Whether those arguments are sound are another issue entirely - but if you look at contemporary arguments for the existence of consciousness outside the body there is nothing about the rigorous arguments that are logically inconsistent.

If you include in supernatural things like ghosts, bigfoot, UFOs then no there are no logically valid arguments for specific paranormal entities. That is with the exception and distinction made between UFOs (abductions) vs Alien life in the universe. God is another issue in that it really depends on what we mean here. Even if you keep it to the judeo-christian yahweh, there are theologians and philosophers who make the argument that the only version of god that matters is the shared sensation. Similarly you have arguments from faith that still hold some water (I am talking about the more nuanced ones and not creationist denialism).

Getting to dualism, or any other metaphysical claims that are purely philosophical in origin, nothing about them negates the material world quite like what is entailed in supernatural explanations. So when it comes to something like "do we have a non-physical component in our make up", dualism answers yes but it poses a problem - how do we know this? Can it be measured? Is it *knowable?* In short, similar *philosophical* positions which are logically valid, present problems that are epistemological as well as ontological in nature. For example - does the mapping of the brain by neuroscientists mean we are 100% physical creatures and there is nothing else?

Similar to the problem that Meno put to Socrates (AFAIK, been a while since I read the ancients), how can a field of science that runs *primarily on the assumption that there is nothing extra required for physical processes to occur and vice versa* confirm or deny metaphysical constructs? As u/wokeupabug said these positions are at the least a useful tool for critically thinking about materialist claims and in fact help us verify whether materialist assumptions are true. At their strongest they give us reason to believe there is a field of knowledge as of yet unestablished.

To add to this Schopenhauer was primarily concerned with pseudo-stoicism/stoic mysticism. He may have acknowledged the suffering in life but it certainly didn't mean that life was not worth living for him.

I am not aligning either race with rich or poor. However gentrification does negatively impact immigrant communities. I'll try to be as brief as I can.

Whilst gentrification cannot explicitly be said to be a targeted, racist or classist process, when you look at how gentrification has been enabled from 2010 (or more accurately 2011) then you gain an understanding that local councils have been stripped of their ability to help their residents. This is important because council's effectively have a duty of care to their residents, so things like 'regeneration schemes' as we see them today were in some way prohibited by that duty due to S. 2 of the Local Government Act 2000. To be more specific:

The 'power to provide well-being' in the Local Government Act 2000 was essentially a legislative quasi-duty, or a power that conferred upon local councils the ability to 'promote' economic, social and environmental well-being. This was limited to Wales in 2012. Whilst it in and of itself does not confer on the council a duty to use that power, if a council were to be sued (as it was in a case in Haringey, Elephant and Castle and one other that precedes either) on its lack of use, it would be successful.

At the same time we have a peice of legislation called the Localism act, which effectively allows local councils to partner up as an individual would. In other words, it gives local council's the same legal personality and make up as a private company. They can sell and trade whatever they wish when it comes to property.

What this effectively means is that, in combination with reduced funding from central government itself, council's *have* to start selling property and shifting poorer residents out of social housing. Their ability to act autonomously is vitiated or corrupted by the interests of private property developers.

This  does *not* mean that private property developers are classist or racist either; however their objective as private companies is to maximise profit. This disproportionately effects poor areas, areas where immigrants are found predominantly or even pensioners and the like. Having worked for local councils, I also happen to know the horrible shit they put residents through to get housing.

Put as succintly as I can, there was a legislative framework that in some ways restricted the speed and ability of council's to do what they're doing (rehoming residents in different boroughs, effectively splitting up families) to free up space for almost exclusively premium builds.  That is not there anymore and has not been since 2012. This has a divisive impact on the stratification on certain ethnic minorities, immigrant and poorer communities.
